title: Dhanush Made a ₹135 Crore Film About a Thief in 1990s Tamil Nadu. It Hit Netflix Today in Five Languages.
excerpt: Kara flopped in theatres. On streaming, it might find the audience it was always meant for — including the NRI one.
body:
Dhanush's latest film *Kara* arrived on Netflix today — May 28, 2026 — in Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, and Hindi. For NRIs who missed its theatrical run in April, this is the first chance to see what might be the most ambitious Tamil film of the year, and one of the most polarizing.

## A ₹135 Crore Gamble on a Slow-Burn Story

Directed by Vignesh Raja, *Kara* is set in early-1990s Tamil Nadu and follows Karasaami, a reformed thief who is forced back into crime after a corrupt bank seizes his family's ancestral land. It is not a masala heist film. It is a slow, deliberate story about systemic injustice, told through the grammar of a thriller — closer in spirit to *Visaranai* than *Dhoom*.

The film cost an estimated ₹135 crore to produce, making it one of the most expensive Tamil films of the year. That budget went into period-accurate production design — the recreation of a 1990s rural Tamil landscape, complete with the bureaucratic architecture of a nationalized banking system that was weaponized against small landowners.

Dhanush delivers what early reviewers called one of his most restrained performances. Karasaami is not a superhero or a romantic lead. He is a man who spent years building a legitimate life, only to have it dismantled by the same system that was supposed to protect him. The supporting cast includes Mamitha Baiju and the Malayalam veteran Jayaram, who plays a quietly devastating role as a bank officer caught between institutional loyalty and personal conscience.

## Why It Struggled in Theatres

*Kara* opened on April 30 against stiff competition and collected approximately ₹52 crore worldwide — a commercial disappointment against its budget, though not an outright disaster. The problem was pacing. Indian audiences in 2026, conditioned by the high-octane energy of films like *Karuppu* and *Drishyam 3*, found *Kara*'s deliberate rhythm difficult to sit through in a theatre.

Critics were kinder. BookMyShow users rated it 8.7 out of 10. Film Twitter called it "the best Tamil film nobody watched." Multiple reviewers compared it to the slow-burn crime thrillers that routinely win international festival prizes but struggle domestically.

## The NRI Streaming Opportunity

This is where Netflix changes the equation. *Kara* is exactly the kind of film that finds its audience on streaming — where the pause button exists, where subtitles in five languages remove the barrier, and where a viewer in New Jersey or Leicester doesn't need to find a theatre showing a Tamil film on opening weekend.

For the Indian diaspora, the film's themes carry extra weight. The story of land being taken by institutional force, of a family's roots being severed by bureaucratic corruption, resonates differently when you are 8,000 miles from the land your grandparents farmed. *Kara* doesn't preach about this. It simply tells a story that lands harder the further you are from home.

Netflix is releasing the film as part of its aggressive 2026 Tamil slate, which already includes streaming deals for *Karuppu* and upcoming rights for Karthi's next film. The platform spent over ₹500 crore on Telugu content alone this year; its Tamil investment is on a similar trajectory.

## The Verdict

*Kara* is not an easy watch. It demands patience. But it is a film made with genuine craft — the kind of mid-budget, director-driven Indian cinema that the NRI audience claims to want more of. Now it's on your screen, in your language, with no excuses left. The question is whether you'll press play.
nri_angle: NRIs who missed Kara's theatrical run now have access in five languages on Netflix — the platform is increasingly becoming the primary way the diaspora watches new Indian cinema.
author: Diaspora Desk
